reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A presynaptic disorder of the neuromuscular junction causing proximal limb weakness, typically most marked in the lower limbs, with a waddling gait
Strength characteristically shows transient post-exercise facilitation, briefly improving after a few seconds of sustained contraction
Autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation, and erectile dysfunction are common and help distinguish it from myasthenia gravis
Reflexes are typically reduced or absent but may become detectable immediately after exercise (post-tetanic potentiation)
Approximately half of cases are paraneoplastic, most often associated with small-cell lung cancer, so a tumour search is essential
Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a low baseline compound muscle action potential with a decrement at low rates and marked increment at high rates or after exercise
Management includes tumour treatment where relevant, symptomatic therapy with 3,4-diaminopyridine, and immunotherapy in refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from autoantibodies directed against presynaptic voltage-gated P/Q-type calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal and in autonomic nerve endings. Reduced calcium influx during the nerve action potential impairs the quantal release of acetylcholine, weakening neuromuscular transmission and producing muscle weakness and autonomic dysfunction. Because more calcium accumulates in the terminal with repeated rapid firing, sustained or high-frequency activity transiently boosts transmitter release, explaining the characteristic post-exercise facilitation of strength and reflexes. In paraneoplastic cases, small-cell lung cancer expresses the same calcium channels, triggering the cross-reactive antibody response.
additionalDifferentials: Guillain-Barre syndrome and chronic inflammatory neuropathies
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing low baseline amplitude with high-frequency or post-exercise increment
CT chest and FDG-PET to detect small-cell lung cancer, with repeat surveillance if initially negative
Single-fibre electromyography where diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Bulbar involvement affecting swallow and airway protection
Positive calcium-channel antibodies indicating high likelihood of underlying malignancy
reference.prognosis: Symptomatic and immunomodulatory treatment often improves strength, and non-paraneoplastic disease may be well controlled long term; in paraneoplastic cases the neurological syndrome frequently improves with successful tumour treatment, though overall prognosis is dominated by the underlying cancer.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as myasthenia gravis and overlooking the autonomic features and post-exercise facilitation
Failing to search for and re-screen for small-cell lung cancer
Misinterpreting reduced reflexes as a peripheral neuropathy
Overlooking drugs that further impair neuromuscular transmission
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Provide symptomatic therapy with amifampridine to prolong nerve-terminal depolarisation and boost acetylcholine release, with pyridostigmine as an adjunct
Identify and treat an underlying malignancy, most often small-cell lung cancer, as tumour-directed treatment frequently improves strength
Add immunomodulation with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents such as azathioprine, or intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange for rapid effect, and rituximab in resistant disease
Repeat surveillance imaging for occult small-cell lung cancer if the initial search is negative in high-risk patients
Offer physiotherapy and manage autonomic dysfunction such as dry mouth, constipation and erectile dysfunction symptomatically
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune disease
Monitor for and escalate care if respiratory or bulbar involvement develops
